reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Infection of the lacrimal sac, usually secondary to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct causing stasis of tears and secretions
Acute dacryocystitis presents with a painful, red, tender swelling at the medial canthus just below the medial canthal tendon, often with epiphora and discharge
Pressure over the sac may express mucopurulent material through the puncta, supporting the diagnosis
The swelling lies below and medial to the medial canthal tendon, which helps distinguish it from preseptal cellulitis and other medial canthal masses
Common organisms include Staphylococcus species and streptococci; management is with systemic antibiotics and warm compresses in the acute phase
Incision and drainage may be needed for a pointing abscess, but definitive treatment of the underlying obstruction is dacryocystorhinostomy once inflammation settles
Congenital dacryocystitis in infants relates to a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner and may need probing if it does not resolve
Acute dacryocystitis can be complicated by preseptal or orbital cellulitis and rarely by fistula formation
reference.pathophysiology: Dacryocystitis is inflammation of the lacrimal sac, almost always resulting from obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct. Obstruction leads to retention and stagnation of tears and mucus within the sac, providing a medium for bacterial overgrowth. Acute infection produces a tense, inflamed sac that may progress to abscess formation, while chronic obstruction causes a mucocele with recurrent low-grade infection and persistent watering. In infants, incomplete canalisation of the duct at the valve of Hasner is the usual cause.
additionalDifferentials: Lacrimal sac tumour (in atypical or bloody presentations)
Infected sebaceous or dermoid cyst at the medial canthus
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination with expression of the lacrimal sac to demonstrate reflux of discharge
Swab of expressed discharge for microscopy, culture, and sensitivities
Syringing and probing of the lacrimal system once acute infection has settled to confirm obstruction
Imaging (CT or dacryocystography) for atypical, recurrent, or mass-like presentations to exclude tumour
redFlags: Spread to preseptal or orbital cellulitis with proptosis, restricted eye movements, or reduced vision
A firm, irregular, or bloody lacrimal sac mass suggesting a lacrimal sac tumour rather than simple infection
Systemic features of sepsis in an unwell patient
Neonatal dacryocystitis, which can progress rapidly and needs prompt treatment
reference.prognosis: Acute dacryocystitis usually responds well to antibiotics, but recurrence is common until the underlying nasolacrimal duct obstruction is corrected surgically; dacryocystorhinostomy is highly effective at relieving obstruction and preventing further episodes.
pitfalls: Attempting probing or surgery during acute inflammation rather than treating the infection first
Mislabelling the medial canthal swelling as preseptal cellulitis and missing the underlying sac infection
Failing to recognise a lacrimal sac tumour presenting as atypical dacryocystitis
Not addressing the underlying duct obstruction, leading to repeated infections
management: Treat acute dacryocystitis with systemic antibiotics covering staphylococci and streptococci, together with warm compresses and analgesia
Send expressed lacrimal sac discharge for microscopy, culture and sensitivities to guide antibiotic choice
Incise and drain a pointing lacrimal sac abscess when one forms
Relieve the underlying nasolacrimal duct obstruction definitively with dacryocystorhinostomy once acute inflammation has settled
In infants, manage congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction with lacrimal sac massage, progressing to probing if it fails to resolve
Escalate urgently with intravenous antibiotics and imaging if postseptal orbital cellulitis is suspected
